sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Non-functional requirements say what the system should be: fast, reliable, usable, secure — the characteristics of functions rather than the functions themselves. The lecture opens with the gap: 'print' alone is not a requirement until you know how fast, how reliably, and measurably how. NFRs close that gap, and the unit tests them harder than any other requirements topic.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: NFRs mostly end in '-ility': usability, security, reliability, and friends. They typically start with 'The system shall...' and attach measurable bounds. They can be listed alongside particular use cases, or held as system-wide constraints in backlogs — but there is no such thing as a purely non-functional use case: a use case as a whole represents a functional requirement.

The worksheet's recognition test is the one to internalise: (1) from the user's point of view, is this a function or a characteristic of a function? (2) Could I write a use-case flow-of-events for it? If you can write the flow, it is functional. If it constrains the flow's qualities, it is non-functional. Then the kicker: 'How could I test it? If you can't test it, it's not valid.'

sections.heading: Why specify NFRs
paras: Because qualities left unspecified get whatever the developers felt like: the lecture's 'for non-superheroes' argument is that ordinary users need guaranteed responsiveness, availability and learnability, not heroic patience. The Gephi SRS shows the professional end-state: performance requirements quantified against a 500 MHz CPU and 128 MB RAM baseline.

articles.summary: NFRs name the system's qualities — testable characteristics of functions, never functions themselves, with no such thing as a purely non-functional use case.
articles.title: Non-functional requirements: overview

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: An NFR nobody can test is decoration, not engineering. The lecture condenses validity into five properties — unambiguous, doable, verifiable, in-scope, and genuinely non-functional — and the 2022 midterm tested them directly: two requirements to demolish, one to rebuild as usable.

sections.heading: The five properties

head: Property
Test
Failure smell
rows: Achievable with available technology and budget
'save images within 1ms' (worksheet item c) — physics says no
Pass/fail decidable by observation; data obtainable
'must be suitable' with no stated test; 'maybe' verdicts from disagreement or unobtainable data
Governs the system, not its actors
'Students cannot enrol after week 1' — a business rule constraining people, not software
Not a function or use-case step in disguise
'System must allow students to see courses' — that is a function (2022 Q3.2a)

paras: Verifiability gets two slides because it fails two ways: people disagree on meaning (ambiguity again), or obtaining enough data is impractical (rare-failure statistics with no observation window). A verdict of 'maybe' means the requirement failed.

sections.heading: Worked demolitions (2022 Q3.2)
paras: (a) 'System must allow students to see available courses and timetable' — invalid because it is functional: from the user's view it is a function, and you could write its flow of events. It may be a fine requirement, but it is miscategorised, and miscategorised requirements escape the measurability discipline NFRs demand.

(b) '...in user friendly manner' — invalid twice over: 'user friendly' is ambiguous (no two markers picture the same threshold) and hence unverifiable (no observation decides pass/fail). The rewrite (Q3.3) must convert friendliness into a measurable usability requirement: pick a user task, a time or effort bound, and a success criterion — e.g. 'An average new user shall locate and display any available ticket type within 60 seconds of first seeing the catalogue, unaided, with at least 9 of 10 succeeding.'

sections.heading: Worksheet traps to rehearse
paras: Item (d) 'must support images up to 100 megapixels' is a capacity characteristic — valid if bounded and testable. Item (e) 'colour enhance within 250 ms on a 10 MP image on an average PC' is the gold-standard shape: operation, bound, workload, environment. Items (h) 'suitable for inclusion in a photo album' and (j) 'must take over 1 minute to open' fail ambiguity and perversity checks respectively. Item (f) crash-rate-per-1000-hours is valid reliability if the failure class and observation method are defined.

articles.summary: Valid NFRs are unambiguous, doable, verifiable, in-scope and truly non-functional — testable constraints, never disguised functions or vibes.
articles.title: What makes an NFR valid

Write down one valid and useful performance requirement for the system. [3 marks]
Gephi requires a system with at least a 500 megahertz CPU and 128 megabytes of RAM...

recall.a: Operation + bound + workload + environment (e.g. enhance 10 MP image within 250 ms on an average PC). hardware factors confound measurement, so fix the environment; stochastic timing needs repeated measurement and statistics.
recall.q: Give the four-part shape of a performance requirement and the two testing caveats.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Performance is software speed under stated conditions — and conditions are half the requirement. Overall performance is as much due to hardware as software, so a bound without an environment ('fast on average PCs' vs 'fast on the ward tablet') is untestable. The 2022 paper's patient-monitor question rewards students who pin all four parts down.

sections.heading: The four-part shape
paras: Operation (what is timed: colour-enhance, chart generation, vital-sign refresh), bound (250 ms, 2 s), workload (10 MP image, 50 concurrent plots), environment (average PC, ward tablet, specified CPU/RAM as in the Gephi SRS). The worksheet's model specimen — 'the colour enhance function shall take at most 250 ms to enhance a 10 MP image on an average PC' — passes every validity property precisely because all four are present.

For the 2022 patient monitor: 'The system shall refresh displayed oxygen level and blood pressure at least once every 2 seconds during continuous monitoring on the ward tablet' — operation, bound, workload, environment, and safety-relevant (stale vitals mislead clinicians).

sections.heading: Testing: stochastic reality
paras: Timing measurements are stochastic: repeated runs give a scatter (#1-#5 in the slides), so verification needs repeated observation and a statistical rule (mean, percentile, worst-of-N) stated in advance — otherwise 'maybe' verdicts return. Fix the hardware, warm the caches, state the percentile: that is what turns a speed wish into a verifiable requirement.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: 'As fast as possible' is not a requirement: no bound, no test.
Single-run timing proves nothing: stochastic measurements need repetitions.
Hardware excuses cut both ways: if the environment is unspecified, the requirement — not the code — is at fault.

articles.summary: Performance requirements bind an operation, a time bound, a workload and an environment — then verify with repeated, statistically-ruled measurement.
articles.title: Performance requirements

List two suitable reliability metrices for the system. [2 marks]
Are (for our purposes) about software reliability, not hardware reliability. Must be based on a kind of measurement that actually makes sense for the particular system.

recall.a: MTTF/MTBF (mean time to/between failures), Availability (uptime fraction), POFOD (probability of failure on demand), ROCOF (failure rate). Choose the metric that fits the usage pattern: POFOD for on-demand checks, availability for continuous monitoring.
recall.q: Name the four reliability metrics and the rule for choosing between them.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Reliability is, basically, the probability the software does its job when asked — but 'when asked' differs by system, so the unit teaches four metrics and insists you choose the one that fits. The 2022 patient monitor and 2019 restaurant questions both punish metric-mismatch: POFOD for a continuous display is as wrong as availability for a rare on-demand check.

sections.heading: The four metrics

head: Metric
Measures
Fits
rows: Fraction of time the service is up
Rate of occurrence of failures over time
Systems with steady failure streams (crash-per-1000-hours style)

paras: The worksheet's three commandments: reliability here means software reliability (not hardware); the metric must make sense for the particular system (hint aimed at POFOD-vs-availability traps); and the requirement states an acceptable failure level for a stated failure class — never perfection, always specific. Systems fail in some ways and not others, and some failures matter more: say which failures you mean.

sections.heading: Worked answers
paras: 2022 Q3.4(b) metrics for the patient monitor: availability ('the display function shall be available at least 99.9% of monitoring time') and ROCOF or MTTF for the sensing pipeline — both fit continuous operation. Q3.4(c) requirement: 'The system shall lose no more than 1 minute of displayed vital-sign data per 24 hours of continuous operation, with any sensor failure annunciated within 5 seconds.' Bound, workload, failure class, detection — every validity property satisfied.

2019 restaurant hint ('not all metrics make sense here'): payment processing is on-demand (POFOD fits), while the kitchen display during service hours is continuous (availability fits). Naming the mismatch explicitly is what the 3 marks buy.

articles.summary: Reliability is failure behaviour quantified: MTTF/MTBF, availability, POFOD, ROCOF — chosen to fit the usage pattern, bounded short of perfection, scoped to a failure class.
articles.title: Reliability requirements and metrics

Propose a useful and valid usability requirement for the system. [3 marks]
Usability requirements are often expressed in terms of what the user must be able to do within a given time, or a given amount of effort. However, be careful to distinguish them from business rules.

recall.a: User task + time/effort bound + success criterion for a stated user class (e.g. average new user completes X within T unaided, 9/10 succeeding). Business rules constrain users; usability requirements describe what the system enables users to do.
recall.q: Give the usability requirement formula and the business-rule distinction.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Usability requirements state what users must be able to do with the system — within a time, or with an effort — thanks to how the system is built. The UI (the part of the system users touch) is where most usability lives, and the lecture offers two measurement approaches: count what users achieve (task success, time-on-task) or assess interface characteristics against principles. Either way, the requirement ends in numbers.

sections.heading: The formula + the trap
paras: User class (average new user, trained cashier) + task (rotate a photo to within 3 degrees of level, locate a ticket type) + bound (within 20 seconds, unaided) + success criterion (9 of 10 succeeding). The worksheet's star specimen: 'an average user must be able, within 20 seconds, to rotate a tilted photograph so that it is within 3 degrees of level.'

The trap is business rules in disguise. 'The user is required to enter a password' constrains the user — a rule. 'An average user shall be able to log in within 30 seconds unaided' describes what the system enables — a usability requirement. The 2019 restaurant usability answer must enable (order a meal within N minutes unaided), never obligate.

sections.heading: Worked answers
paras: 2019 restaurant: 'An average first-time customer shall complete a standard order and card payment within 5 minutes of pressing start, unaided, with at least 9 of 10 succeeding in evaluation.' 2022 ticketing rewrite: same shape, ticket-type task. Both name the user class (average/first-time), the task, the bound, and the bar — which is exactly the hidden mark scheme.

articles.summary: Usability requirements quantify what defined users can achieve within what time or effort — system-enabled ability, never user obligations.
articles.title: Usability requirements

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Beyond the big three (performance, reliability, usability) sit security, interoperability, localisation and accessibility — each with its own lecture slide and a standing invitation in Worksheet 4 Q5. The 2022 paper's finale (Q3.4d) asks you to propose one such parameter for the patient monitor, justify it, and write its requirement: 6 marks for judgement plus craft.

sections.heading: The four, briefly
bullets: Security — everyone's responsibility: authentication, authorisation, audit. Vitals are health data; unauthorised display or alteration harms patients.
Interoperability — software must work with other software: export vitals to the hospital EHR in an agreed format.
Localisation (L10N) — adapt language, units, culture: ward staff across campuses need consistent units and terminology.
Accessibility — cater for diverse abilities: alarms perceivable by staff with hearing or vision limits; operable gloved and one-handed.
paras: Exam move in two steps: (1) parameter + reason tied to the system ('security, because vitals are confidential health data on a shared ward display'); (2) quantified requirement ('the system shall lock the display after 60 s idle and require badge re-authentication; unauthorised access attempts shall be logged with timestamp and user ID'). Judgement first, numbers second.

articles.summary: Security, interoperability, localisation and accessibility complete the NFR palette — propose the parameter that fits the system's risks, then quantify it.
articles.title: Security, interoperability, localisation, accessibility

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: The Software Requirements Specification is the document listing all requirements — and IEEE 830 is the standard describing what a good one looks like. The lecture lifts its layout wholesale (introduction, overall description, interfaces, functional requirements, NFRs), and the Gephi SRS shows a real one in the wild. Midterm questions rarely ask IEEE by name, but every 'write a valid requirement' mark is secretly graded against it.

sections.heading: A good SRS (IEEE 4.3)
paras: Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked for importance/stability, verifiable, modifiable, traceable. Two of these do quiet exam work: ranked (not all requirements matter equally — the Product Backlog's ordering is ranking made agile) and traceable (each requirement linkable to its source and its tests — the ancestor of this wiki's citations). The standard's hall of shame for verifiability — 'works well', 'good human interface', 'shall usually happen' — is the same family as the lecture's 'user friendly' and the worksheet's 'suitable for photo albums'. Learn to hear the register: unmeasurable adjectives are failed requirements.

sections.heading: Layout you should recognise
paras: Introduction (purpose, scope, definitions/acronyms), overall description (the general factors affecting the product — not requirements themselves), external interfaces (system/user/hardware/software/communications), functional requirements by mode/class/object, performance requirements, design constraints, system attributes (reliability, availability, security per section 5.3.6), and supporting material (contents, index, appendixes). The Gephi SRS follows this skeleton across 37 pages — skim its table of contents once and the abstract standard becomes concrete.

articles.summary: IEEE 830 defines the SRS contract: eight virtues with verifiability as the teeth, and a section layout the course reuses for stories, cases and NFRs.

sections.heading: How NFR marks are lost
bullets: Calling a function an NFR (2022 Q3.2a, 2019 Q3c-ii counting statistics).
Calling a business rule an NFR (2019 Q3c-i kitchen timing governs staff).
Leaving 'user friendly' unquantified instead of rewriting with user/task/bound/criterion.
Proposing a reliability metric that mismatches usage (POFOD for continuous monitoring).
Writing 'perfect reliability' or unbounded performance ('as fast as possible').
Omitting the environment from performance bounds.
